new-mexico.agency_name: New Mexico Children, Youth & Families Department (CYFD)
new-mexico.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18 under the New Mexico Children's Code, when CYFD custody generally ends. CYFD's Fostering Connections program then offers voluntary extended support.
new-mexico.become_foster_parent: Contact CYFD to express interest and start the process; CYFD will connect you with a representative or regional navigator. Applicants complete eligibility checks, a SAFE home study, background checks, and pre-service training, and are licensed through CYFD, with the license renewed every two years.
new-mexico.benefits_after: Fostering Connections provides Medicaid, help paying for college, housing support (including Transitional Living for Young Adults, Transitions Supportive Housing, and Foster Youth Independence housing help), job help, and food access for youth ages 18 to 26. Youth who were in foster care at 18 can also keep Medicaid to age 26 and may qualify for federal Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training.
new-mexico.extended_care: Yes — New Mexico offers extended foster care to age 21 through Fostering Connections, created by 2019 legislation and fully in place by 2023. A youth who was in care at 18 can stay in or re-enter care to 21 by signing a Voluntary Services and Support Agreement and meeting one activity condition, such as finishing school, being in college or job training, working, or having a medical condition that prevents those activities.
new-mexico.foster_overview: The Children, Youth & Families Department (CYFD), through its Protective Services Division, places children who cannot safely stay at home into foster care, usually after a court order. Foster parents (called resource foster parents) give children a safe, stable home and daily care while CYFD works toward reunification or another permanent plan.
new-mexico.kinship_care: Yes — relatives and fictive kin can foster, and kinship placements are about half of New Mexico placements. Kinship caregivers can become licensed resource foster parents, and the Kinship Guardianship Program links grandparents and other relatives raising children to navigators, training, support groups, and free legal help.

new-york.agency_name: New York State Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS)
new-york.aging_out_age: Youth age out at 18, when placement generally cannot continue without the youth's consent, under Family Court Act sections 1055(e) and 756-a(f). No placement may continue past age 21.
new-york.become_foster_parent: Apply through your local department of social services or an authorized voluntary foster care agency, starting with OCFS's foster care inquiry process. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks and a home study, and complete required training before certification.
new-york.benefits_after: Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. The Chafee Foster Care Program for Successful Transition to Adulthood offers life-skills, education, employment, and housing help, generally from age 14 to 21 (and to 23 for youth who aged out at 18-20), and the Education and Training Voucher program offers up to $5,000 a year for college or vocational training, with eligibility to age 26 if first awarded before 21.
new-york.extended_care: Yes — youth may remain in foster care to age 21 if they consent, under Family Court Act sections 1055(e) and 1091. Youth who leave care after 18 can also ask to re-enter before age 21 (within 24 months of discharge), if they have no reasonable alternative to foster care and agree to enroll in school or vocational training, unless that is unnecessary for their situation.
new-york.foster_overview: Foster care in New York is supervised statewide by the Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS) and run locally by county departments of social services and authorized voluntary agencies, under Family Court orders. Foster parents care for children in their homes, keep them connected to family, and support the plan for reunification or another permanent home.
new-york.kinship_care: Yes — relatives and certain non-relatives can be approved as kinship foster parents, and New York gives first consideration to placing a child with relatives. Kinship caregivers can also receive help through the Kinship Navigator program and, in some cases, the Kinship Guardianship Assistance Program (KinGAP).

north-carolina.agency_name: North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Social Services
north-carolina.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18 under N.C.G.S. 131D-10.2B, which also authorizes continued foster care services to age 21. A youth who opts out at 18 may later opt back in before turning 21.
north-carolina.become_foster_parent: Contact your county department of social services or a licensed private foster care agency, watch the mandatory orientation video, and complete the licensing process. Applicants must be at least 21, complete 30 hours of training, pass background checks, and complete a mutual home assessment for licensing, renewed every two years.
north-carolina.benefits_after: Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. The program also provides casework, a transition living plan, placement support, and help with education and employment, and former foster youth may qualify for federal Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) and Chafee independent-living services.
north-carolina.extended_care: Yes — North Carolina's Foster Care 18 to 21 program lets a youth who was in foster care on their 18th birthday stay in or return to care until 21. The youth must sign a voluntary placement agreement with a county department and meet one condition: finishing high school or an equivalent, being in college or vocational school, being in a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a medical condition or disability.
north-carolina.foster_overview: County departments of social services place children in foster care under the supervision of the state Division of Social Services (NCDHHS), after a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home. Foster parents provide a temporary, safe home and daily care while the county works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
north-carolina.kinship_care: Yes — kinship foster care is the preferred placement when a child must be removed, and kin can be relatives by birth or a person with a family-like relationship. Kinship caregivers do not have to be licensed to care for a child, but becoming licensed (with a reduced 15-hour NTDC training option for relatives) qualifies them for monthly financial help and, in some cases, the Kinship Guardianship Assistance Program (KinGAP).

north-dakota.agency_name: North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services, Children and Family Services
north-dakota.aging_out_age: Youth age out at 18, when the child-in-need-of-protection court order terminates under N.D. Cent. Code 27-20.3-26 and the youth is discharged from custody. Youth who want to keep receiving help can move into the 18+ Continued Care program.
north-dakota.become_foster_parent: Contact the North Dakota Children and Family Services licensing unit or a local Human Service Zone to start the process. Applicants must be at least 21, pass fingerprint-based criminal background and child abuse/neglect checks, provide references, complete a home study and required training (about 30 hours), and complete fire-prevention training.
north-dakota.benefits_after: Youth who were in North Dakota foster care and on Medicaid when they turned 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26 regardless of income. The Chafee Program offers independent-living services, flex funds, and room-and-board funds to youth up to age 23, and Education and Training Vouchers of up to $5,000 a year (lifetime maximum $25,000) for college or vocational training, available to apply for up to age 26.
north-dakota.extended_care: Yes — North Dakota's 18+ Continued Care program is available to eligible youth up to age 21 under N.D. Cent. Code 27-20-30.1. The youth must have aged out while under a court order to a North Dakota public agency, Tribal social services, or the Division of Juvenile Services, sign the 18+ Continued Foster Care Agreement, and meet an education, employment, employment-preparation, or medical-condition condition; youth can return within six months of discharge.
north-dakota.foster_overview: Foster care in North Dakota is run by the Department of Health and Human Services, Children and Family Services, working with local Human Service Zones, Tribal social services, and the Division of Juvenile Services. When a court finds a child needs protection, the agency places the child in a licensed foster home, with the goal of reunification when it is safe.
north-dakota.kinship_care: Yes — relatives and other adults with a close relationship to the child can care for them as kinship caregivers, and no foster license is required for relative/kinship care, though a background check and home safety check are done. Kinship caregivers can get support through the Kinship-ND program, and children placed with relatives within the fifth degree may qualify for TANF Kinship Care funding.

ohio.aging_out_age: Youth age out at 18, when custody of the public children services agency generally ends, under Ohio Rev. Code 2151.81. Eligible youth can then choose the voluntary Bridges program instead of leaving support behind.
ohio.become_foster_parent: Start at FosterAndAdopt.ohio.gov or contact your county public children services agency or a private child-placing agency to choose an agency and begin certification. Applicants complete an application, background checks with fingerprinting, references, a home study, and 24 to 36 hours of pre-placement training.
ohio.benefits_after: Youth who age out of foster care in Ohio can keep Medicaid until age 26. Bridges provides help with stable housing, education, employment, and community resources, and former foster youth can apply for Education and Training Vouchers of up to $5,000 a year for college or job training, as well as independent-living services through their county agency.
ohio.extended_care: Yes — Ohio's Bridges program, created by 2016 House Bill 50, supports young adults from 18 to 21 who emancipated from a PCSA, a Title IV-E juvenile court, or the Department of Youth Services. To qualify, the young adult must be finishing secondary school, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a physical or mental health condition.
ohio.foster_overview: Foster care in Ohio is run by county public children services agencies (PCSAs) under the Ohio Department of Children & Youth, with courts ordering placement when a child cannot safely stay at home. Foster parents provide a temporary home and daily care while the agency works toward reunification with the birth family or, if that is not possible, adoption.
ohio.kinship_care: Yes — a relative's home is the first choice for a child who needs temporary care in Ohio. Kinship caregivers can receive Kinship Support Program payments for up to six months while they work toward foster-care certification, and licensed kinship caregivers can receive foster care payments and help from the Ohio Kinship and Adoption Navigator (OhioKAN).

oklahoma.aging_out_age: Youth age out of foster care at 18, when OKDHS custody generally ends. Oklahoma's Successful Adulthood services were already available to youth in care from age 14, and a new extended foster care law now carries support to 21.
oklahoma.become_foster_parent: Contact Oklahoma Human Services' Foster Care and Adoption Support Center or visit okfosters.org to start the process. Applicants must be at least 21, financially stable without relying on foster care payments, pass background checks for household members age 13 and older, and complete required training and a home assessment.
oklahoma.benefits_after: The Oklahoma Successful Adulthood Program (OKSA) helps youth in and from foster care with independent-living skills, education, employment, and housing as they move toward adulthood. Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26, and former foster youth up to age 26 may qualify for Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training.
oklahoma.extended_care: Yes — Senate Bill 1806, signed in 2026 and effective July 1, 2026, created extended foster care to age 21 in Oklahoma. Eligible young adults who were in OKDHS custody at 18, or who reached permanency through guardianship or adoption at age 16 or older and no longer have caregiver support, can voluntarily continue services to 21 by finishing secondary school, being in college or career-tech, being in an employment-readiness program, working at least 80 hours a month, or having a documented medical condition that prevents those activities; services can include Medicaid, a monthly stipend, and continued caseworker support.
oklahoma.foster_overview: Oklahoma Human Services (OKDHS), Child Welfare Services, places children in foster care when a court finds they cannot safely stay at home because of abuse or neglect. Foster parents provide 24-hour temporary care in a home setting while OKDHS works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
oklahoma.kinship_care: Yes — Oklahoma has a Kinship Foster Care Program under 10A O.S. 1-9-106, and OKDHS must try to place a removed child with a person who has a kinship relationship with the child, including relatives by blood, marriage, or adoption and people with a close emotional tie or bond. Kinship foster parents complete training (at least 12 hours, within 120 days of placement where possible) and background checks, and can receive foster care payments once finally approved.

oregon.agency_name: Oregon Department of Human Services (ODHS), Child Welfare
oregon.aging_out_age: Youth generally age out at 18, when the court may dismiss their case, but a ward's commitment to ODHS can continue until the court dismisses it or the youth turns 21, under ORS 419B.337(6). In practice, most youth who emancipate leave care at 18.
oregon.become_foster_parent: Contact ODHS Child Welfare through its partner Every Child Oregon, which recruits and supports resource families, to start the certification process. Applicants must generally be at least 21, pass child-abuse and criminal background checks, have space and financial resources to support their household, and complete orientation and Foundations/RAFT training.
oregon.benefits_after: Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. ODHS transition services (the Independent Living Program) help youth age 14 and older, and former foster youth under 24, with life skills, education, employment, housing help including an independent-living housing subsidy, and flexible funds, and former foster youth may qualify for Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training.
oregon.extended_care: Yes — Oregon offers extended foster care to age 21. Under ORS 419B.337 and ODHS rule OAR 413-030-0220, a young adult can stay in substitute care to 21 if staying in care is in their best interest and they are working toward high school graduation or a GED, employed, in a training program, in approved volunteer work, in a special-education program, or an unaccompanied refugee minor; Oregon law does not allow re-entry once a youth has left care.
oregon.foster_overview: The Oregon Department of Human Services (ODHS), Child Welfare, places children in foster care when a judge finds home is not safe, with the goal of reunifying the family whenever possible. Children live with resource families (foster parents), relatives, or specialized programs while birth families get help to stabilize.
oregon.kinship_care: Yes — placing a child with relatives is the preferred option in Oregon, and relatives can become certified resource parents for a child in their family. Relatives are notified by ODHS when a child enters care, and kinship caregivers can get help through ODHS Relative and Kinship Connections and local Child Welfare offices.

pennsylvania.agency_name: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Children, Youth and Families
pennsylvania.aging_out_age: Youth age out at 18, when dependency jurisdiction generally ends, but under Act 91 (42 Pa.C.S. 6302) a youth adjudicated dependent before 18 can ask the court to retain jurisdiction to age 21. Youth whose jurisdiction ended within 90 days before turning 18, or on or after 18, may also seek resumption of jurisdiction.
pennsylvania.become_foster_parent: Contact your county children and youth agency or a licensed private foster care agency to start the process. Applicants must be at least 21, pass criminal, child-abuse, and FBI background checks for everyone in the home age 14 and older, pass a medical appraisal and home evaluation, and complete agency training and a home study.
pennsylvania.benefits_after: Youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26. Pennsylvania's Chafee Independent Living Program serves youth in care ages 14 to 21 and offers aftercare services to age 23, including life-skills training, education and employment help, housing location and room-and-board help; the Chafee Education and Training Grant offers up to $5,000 a year for college or career school, and the Fostering Independence Tuition Waiver (FosterED) can waive tuition at Pennsylvania schools for eligible former foster youth.
pennsylvania.extended_care: Yes — Pennsylvania offers extended foster care to age 21 under Act 91. A youth under 21 who aged out within 90 days of turning 18 or after 18 can remain in or re-enter care by meeting one activity condition: completing secondary school or an equivalent, being in college or vocational school, being in a program to promote or remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a medical or behavioral health condition.
pennsylvania.foster_overview: Foster care in Pennsylvania is state-supervised by the Department of Human Services' Office of Children, Youth and Families and administered by the 67 county children and youth agencies, under court orders. Foster parents give children a temporary, safe home and daily care while the county works toward reunification or another permanent plan.
pennsylvania.kinship_care: Yes — Pennsylvania law requires the county agency to give first consideration to placing a child with relatives or kin, including a godparent or someone with an existing meaningful relationship. Relatives can serve as kinship foster parents, and kinship guardianship subsidies and adoption subsidies can be extended to age 21 for eligible youth under Act 80.

rhode-island.agency_name: Rhode Island Department of Children, Youth & Families (DCYF)
rhode-island.aging_out_age: Youth age out at 18, when Family Court jurisdiction generally ends under R.I. Gen. Laws 14-1-6, unless the youth elects the Voluntary Extension of Care program. DCYF must present a transition plan covering housing, health insurance, education or employment, mentors, and support services six months before a youth turns 18.
rhode-island.become_foster_parent: Apply through DCYF's Resource Families program, using its online BINTI applicant portal, or through a licensed community partner agency. Applicants must generally be at least 21 (kinship caregivers ages 18 to 20 may be considered), pass background checks, be in good enough health and financially able to care for a child, pass fire and safety (and lead, where required) inspections, and complete 30 hours of pre-service training and a home study.
rhode-island.benefits_after: Youth who were in foster care on their 18th birthday can keep Medicaid to age 21 under DCYF's aftercare rules, and youth who were in foster care at 18 can keep Medicaid to age 26 under federal former-foster-youth coverage. DCYF and its partner Foster Forward provide aftercare services, housing and employment help, and postsecondary education assistance to youth ages 18 to 21, and former foster youth may qualify for Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) for college or job training.
rhode-island.extended_care: Yes — Rhode Island's Voluntary Extension of Care (VEC) program lets a youth who was in DCYF legal custody at 18 voluntarily stay under DCYF care and Family Court supervision to age 21, under R.I. Gen. Laws 14-1-6. The youth must sign a voluntary placement agreement and meet one condition: finishing high school or a GED, being in secondary or postsecondary/vocational education, being in job training or a program to remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a documented medical condition; youth who leave VEC can ask to be reinstated before 21.
rhode-island.foster_overview: The Rhode Island Department of Children, Youth and Families (DCYF) is the single state agency that places children in foster care when the Family Court finds they cannot safely stay at home. Foster parents, called resource parents, give children a safe, nurturing home while DCYF works toward reunification or another permanent plan.
rhode-island.kinship_care: Yes — when DCYF gets temporary custody of a child, it must investigate placing the child with a fit and willing relative, under R.I. Gen. Laws 14-1-27. Relatives can be certified as kinship resource parents, with some licensing rules eased for relatives, and kinship caregivers ages 18 to 20 may be considered where other applicants must be 21.

south-carolina.agency_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services (DSS)
south-carolina.aging_out_age: Youth age out at 18, the age of majority, when DSS custody generally ends. South Carolina's extended foster care law, S.C. Code 63-7-2710 and following (Article 8, added in 2022), lets eligible youth stay under DSS placement and care to age 21.
south-carolina.become_foster_parent: Choose a licensing partner (a private child-placing agency, or DSS in some circumstances) through DSS's foster care pages and complete the licensing process. Applicants complete an application, required pre-service training, criminal and central-registry background checks and fingerprinting for household members 18 and older, a home study, references, medical reports, and fire, health, sanitation, and lead inspections.
south-carolina.benefits_after: Youth who were in foster care on their 18th birthday can keep Medicaid to age 26. DSS's Chafee program provides casework, help finishing high school, education and employment help, housing and financial-management help, and aftercare services to former foster youth up to age 26, and Education and Training Vouchers (up to $5,000 a year) help pay for college or vocational school.
south-carolina.extended_care: Yes — South Carolina extends foster care to age 21 under S.C. Code 63-7-2710 to 63-7-2770 and DSS Policy 546. A youth who was in DSS legal custody on their 18th birthday can sign a Voluntary Placement Agreement to stay in or return to care before 21, and must meet one condition: finishing secondary school or an equivalent, being in college or vocational school, being in a program to promote or remove barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or being unable to do those things because of a physical, intellectual, emotional, or psychiatric condition.
south-carolina.foster_overview: The South Carolina Department of Social Services (DSS) places children in foster care when the Family Court finds they cannot safely stay at home because of abuse or neglect. Foster parents provide temporary care in a home setting while DSS works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
south-carolina.kinship_care: Yes — DSS must try to identify a relative or fictive kin for placement when a child is removed, under S.C. Code 63-7-2320, and preference is given to a relative or person known to the child with a caring relationship. Kin can become licensed kinship foster parents, which brings the full foster care board rate, Medicaid for the child, and child-care vouchers; kinship care coordinators in each region help caregivers through licensing and local resources.
